problem.text: Let $\lfloor x\rfloor$ denote the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$. How many real numbers $x$ satisfy the equation $x^2+10{,}000\lfloor x\rfloor=10{,}000x$?

steps.title: Where to start: spot the fractional part
steps.body: The equation has both $x$ and $\lfloor x\rfloor$ with the same coefficient $10{,}000$, which is a hint to group them. The difference $x-\lfloor x\rfloor$ is called the fractional part of $x$: it is how far $x$ is above the integer just below it (or equal to it), so it is always at least $0$ and less than $1$. For example, the fractional part of $3.7$ is $0.7$, and of $-2.3$ it is $0.7$ too, since $\lfloor -2.3\rfloor=-3$.

your_turn.prompt: Move terms and divide by $10{,}000$. What does the equation say?
your_turn.answer: $\frac{x^2}{10000}=x-\lfloor x\rfloor$: the fractional part of $x$ equals $\frac{x^2}{10000}$.

steps.title: Solutions can only be in a limited range
steps.body: The right side is a fractional part, so it lies in $[0,1)$. That means the left side $\frac{x^2}{10000}$ must also be less than $1$. This already rules out all large $x$, positive or negative.

your_turn.answer: $x^2<10000$, so $-100<x<100$. In particular $x=\pm100$ are not solutions.

steps.title: One stretch at a time
steps.body: Split the line into stretches $[n,n+1)$ with $n$ an integer. On each stretch the fractional part is $x-n$: it starts at $0$ and climbs toward $1$ with slope $1$. Meanwhile, for $|x|<100$ the curve $\frac{x^2}{10000}$ has slope $\frac{x}{5000}$, smaller than $\frac{1}{50}$ in size, so it barely moves. So on a stretch the fractional part catches up with the curve at most once, and it does catch up if the curve is still below $1$ when $x$ reaches the right end $n+1$.

your_turn.prompt: At the left end $x=n$ of a stretch, which is bigger: the fractional part or $\frac{x^2}{10000}$?
your_turn.answer: The fractional part is $0$ and $\frac{n^2}{10000}\ge0$, so the curve is at or above it (equal only when $n=0$, giving the solution $x=0$).

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body: A stretch $[n,n+1)$ has exactly one solution when $(n+1)^2<10000$, that is $-101<n<99$, and none otherwise. Careful at the top: on $[99,100)$ the curve reaches $1$ only at $x=100$, which is not in the stretch, so it has no solution. The bottom stretch $[-100,-99)$ does have one, since $\frac{99^2}{10000}<1$. So $n$ runs from $-100$ to $98$, which is $98-(-100)+1=199$ stretches with one solution each. The answer is **(C)**.

wrong_choices.D: $200$ counts every stretch from $n=-100$ to $n=99$. On $[99,100)$ the curve $\frac{x^2}{10000}$ reaches $1$ only at $x=100$, which is not included, so that stretch has no solution.
wrong_choices.E: $201$ comes from also counting $x=100$ and $x=-100$ as solutions. At both, the fractional part is $0$ but $\frac{x^2}{10000}=1$, so they fail.
